messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Writer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Before the accident, Arjun had thought of himself as someone who noticed things. He was a writer, after all—he paid attention to the details other people missed: the way light fell across a room, the cadence of a friend’s laugh, the small, unspoken rhythms of daily life. That was what made his stories feel alive. But now, noticing things had become a curse. Every creak of the floorboards in his apartment, every sudden clatter from the kitchen, every unexpected sound sent a jolt through his chest that left him breathless and shaking. He had started sleeping with the television on, not because it helped him relax—he could not relax anywhere, not even in his own bed—but because the constant drone of noise felt safer than the silence, which was punctuated by sounds that made him feel as though something terrible was about to happen again.

The terrible thing had happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. Arjun’s older brother, Ravi, had been riding his bicycle home from work along a road they had both taken a hundred times. A driver ran a red light. By the time Arjun got to the hospital, Ravi was already gone. There was no warning, no slow decline, no chance to say goodbye. Just a phone call, a taxi ride, and a room where a doctor used words that did not seem to belong to Arjun’s life. In the weeks that followed, Arjun had tried to hold onto the belief that the world made sense—that bad things happened for reasons, that there was some order beneath the chaos—but that belief had shattered completely. He no longer trusted that the world was safe. He no longer trusted that anything was safe. He had come to believe that disaster was simply waiting, hidden behind ordinary moments, and that he was powerless to see it coming.

He stopped making plans. Not just big plans, like travel or career goals, but any plans at all. When a friend asked if he wanted to grab coffee next week, Arjun said he would let them know, and then he never did. When his editor asked about his next project, he said he was still thinking about it. The truth was that thinking about the future felt like tempting fate. Every time he imagined a happy event—a holiday, a dinner out, a quiet weekend—he was certain that something would happen to destroy it. It was safer to live in the present, or better yet, in the past, where the worst thing had already happened and could not happen again.

But the past was not safe either. Grief reminders were everywhere. The smell of Ravi’s favorite curry from the Indian restaurant down the street made Arjun’s stomach turn. The sight of a bicycle locked to a rack outside a shop made him cross to the other side of the road. He had stopped going to the park where they used to play chess on Sunday afternoons. He had stopped answering calls from his mother, because her voice sounded too much like Ravi’s. He knew she was worried about him, but every time she asked if he was okay, he felt a desperate urge to ask her the same question back, over and over, as if her reassurance might somehow stick. He kept asking his roommate, his remaining friends, even the barista at the coffee shop where he used to write—“Do I look okay? Do I seem normal?”—but the answers never lasted. The fear always came back.

He had once been a happy person. He remembered that version of himself the way one remembers a character from a book read long ago. That Arjun had laughed easily, had looked forward to things, had believed that the world was basically good. That Arjun was gone. In his place was someone who jumped at the sound of a car horn, who lay awake at three in the morning staring at the ceiling, who could not imagine a single future event without feeling a cold certainty that it would never come to pass. He came to therapy because his roommate had finally sat him down and said, “You cannot keep living like this.” Arjun did not know if he could live any other way. But he was tired. He was so tired. And for the first time in months, he let himself hope that maybe, just maybe, there was a way back to the world he had lost.
